profiles.meeting_scenario: At a mid-sized quantitative trading technology firm, two leads are holding a brainstorming meeting about how to turn an internal research methodology for statistically uniform evaluation of automated trading platform components into a marketable evaluation offering for institutional clients. The context is that the firm has a research prototype demonstrating hypothesis-test-based evaluation of trading patterns and feature extraction modules on a US futures instrument, and leadership wants ideas for packaging it as a repeatable capability across the firm's platform. The agenda is to generate candidate ways to position, scope, and pilot the methodology for clients without locking into detailed implementation yet. The expected outcome is a short list of promising concept directions for a pilot offering, plus rough agreement on what the first external-facing version would cover.

members.name: Alicia Chen
members.expertise: Statistical evaluation of trading signals, market microstructure, and research reproducibility
members.background: Alicia leads the firm's research group and previously worked as a quantitative researcher at a futures trading shop, where she built validation pipelines for signal libraries and internal model governance.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the methodological rigor of the research and avoid the offering being diluted into a marketing scorecard that overpromises what the statistics can support.
hidden_assumptions: A 'comparable' evaluation means the methodology controls for instrument and sample differences well enough that researchers can make defensible cross-study judgments, not merely place results side by side.

When people say 'platform components' in this context, they primarily mean alpha-generating research modules such as pattern detectors, feature extraction steps, and signal transforms rather than downstream execution or risk controls.
The natural first pilot is the same ES rolling front-month futures setup used in the research prototype, because continuity with the existing evidence base matters more than commercial visibility.
A 'reproducibility pack' should let an internal or client quant independently rerun the statistical workflow with code, seeds, window definitions, and test settings.
If something is 'interpretable to practitioners,' a buy-side quant or desk analyst can understand effect sizes, null-hypothesis framing, and decision implications after a short walkthrough.

members.name: Daniel Ruiz
members.expertise: Packaging quantitative capabilities for clients, pilot design, and platform commercialization
members.background: Daniel manages external-facing product strategy for the firm's automated trading platform and previously worked in enterprise fintech product roles focused on turning research tools into client-ready offerings.
members.private_state: He wants a pilot concept that sales can position quickly with existing client demand and that feels broad enough to justify a commercial roadmap beyond a narrow research use case.
hidden_assumptions: A 'comparable' evaluation means clients can view different components on a common scorecard and make fast side-by-side purchase or deployment decisions.
When people say 'platform components,' that includes not only signal modules but also execution logic, risk overlays, and any configurable block the client sees inside the trading stack.
The natural first pilot is the June client-facing futures pilot around Micro E-mini exposure, because that is the commercially active opportunity people internally are already referring to.
A 'reproducibility pack' is mainly a client-facing methodology artifact that shows consistency and auditability without requiring distribution of executable research code.
If something is 'interpretable to practitioners,' a portfolio manager, sales engineer, or risk committee member should grasp it from a concise visual explanation without needing statistical training.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly discuss making the evaluation 'uniform and comparable' across components.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Alicia means statistically comparable in the research sense: normalized and controlled enough that results from different studies or instruments can be interpreted with defensible methodological consistency.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means commercially comparable in the product sense: different components can be shown on one client-facing scorecard so buyers can compare them at a glance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are positive, compatible-sounding, and common in business conversations; each speaker hears the other's comments as support for the same broad goal of standardization.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They talk about extending the methodology to 'other platform components.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Alicia assumes the scope includes upstream research artifacts like trading patterns, feature extractors, and signal-generation modules, because those are what the methodology was designed to evaluate.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel assumes the scope includes any client-visible module in the platform, including execution schedulers, risk guards, and portfolio overlays, since those are all sold as components.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is already embedded in company language, so neither expects it to need unpacking; both can give examples that sound reasonable without exposing that their boundaries differ.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'the futures pilot' or 'the June pilot' as the obvious first proving ground.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Alicia is thinking of the internal ES rolling front-month futures research setup used in the prototype and paper-like validation workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel is thinking of the upcoming client pilot centered on Micro E-mini futures, which sales has been informally calling the June futures pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both pilots involve US equity index futures and are salient recent initiatives, so shorthand references like 'the futures pilot' feel unambiguous even though they point to different concrete setups.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes the methodology 'practitioner-friendly' and reproducible
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss creating a 'practitioner-friendly reproducibility pack.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Alicia thinks success means a quant practitioner can rerun the workflow, inspect hypothesis tests, and reproduce effect-size tables with the same settings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel thinks success means a practitioner can trust the process from a concise methodology note, templated report, and governance summary without touching code.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria point to transparency and usability, so they sound like the same aspiration; the conflict only appears later when deciding what artifacts must actually be included.

If this becomes just a glossy ranking sheet, we'll lose the rigor that made the prototype valuable in the first place.
